A dissolved oxygen concentration of 5.0 mg/l has been used by the Southeast Reservoir Investigations (Clugston, 1976) and the South Carolina Wildlife and Marine Resources Department (Timmerman, 1976) in assessments of optimum trout habitat. Applicant (Appendix J, Exhibit W) also used this level in some of its analyses of trout habitat thickness.
Trout would be expected to survive at dissolved oxygen concentrations as low as 3.0 mg/l. However, this level, in combination with temperatures at or near the maximum level for trout, would be expected to create greater stress than either low dissolved oxygen concentrations or high temperatures individually, and could be expected to have an adverse impact on normal growth and development. Dissolved oxygen concentrations of 4.0 mg/l at non-stressful temperatures would easily allow for the survival of trout and probably also for reasonably good growth. Conversely, continued exposure to a temperature of 70°F. and a DO level of 3.0 mg/l on a sustained basis would have an adverse effect on trout. Thus, 3.0 mg/l might be acceptable as an absolute minimum DO concentration in the absence of high temperatures. In Lake Jocassee, for example, water deep enough to contain only 3.0 mg/l DO concentration is usually considerably cooler than 70°F.
During the portions of the year when Lake Jocassee is essentially unstratified, trout habitat extends from the surface to great depth, limited only by the low DO levels in the deep waters that sometimes remain even during the winter period. As warming occurs and the reservoir becomes thermally stratified, trout habitat becomes restricted to a band of water having adequate DO and low enough temperatures. This band of trout water becomes shaller as the summer progresses and eventually reaches a minimum in late summer or early fall (Figure 2-20). During the summer of 1975, optimum trout habitat (20°C; 5.0 mg/l of DO) was eliminated for a brief period during late September and early October. When a DO criterion of 4.0 mg/l is substituted, habitat remains throughout the season, although a reduction in size still occurs as summer progresses.
The data also show that the thickness of the band of trout water is less in tributary arms of the reservoir than in the more central regions (Figure 2-21). This effect has been reported for other reservoirs that support two-story fisheries (Baker and Mathis, 1968; Wilkins, et al., 1967).
